name: K-Means Clustering
miniText: How can repeated assignment and averaging divide observations into groups? NetLogo K-Means Clustering creates points, initializes centroids, assigns points to their closest centroid, and relocates centroids toward the means of their assigned groups. Lloyd [1] supplies the least-squares quantization method, Hartigan and Wong [2] develop a major k-means algorithm, and Jain [3] reviews the assumptions and limitations of clustering. The model distinguishes the number of generating groups from the number of centroids requested by the user. Initialization, Euclidean distance, outliers, and the chosen value of k affect the result. Different runs can settle on different partitions, and visually plausible groups need not recover a unique underlying truth. The experiment illustrates optimization of a geometric within-group criterion, rather than proving that every dataset contains spherical clusters or that convergence identifies the global minimum.
